lessons.summary: Explain how limited resources create choices, opportunity costs and competing priorities.
objectives: Distinguish scarcity from a temporary shortage.
Identify opportunity cost.
Evaluate choices using stakeholder evidence.
keyIdeas: Scarcity exists because wants exceed available resources.
Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative forgone.
A choice can distribute costs and benefits unevenly.

definitions.meaning: The condition in which available resources cannot satisfy every possible want.
The value of the next-best alternative given up.
A person or group affected by a decision.

method: Identify the limited resource.
Name the realistic alternatives.
State the next-best alternative forgone.
Compare effects across stakeholders and time.

workedExample.prompt: A council uses vacant land for a sports centre instead of affordable housing.
steps: The scarce resource is usable urban land.
The chosen use is the sports centre.
If housing was the next-best option, its benefits are the opportunity cost.
workedExample.conclusion: The decision cannot be judged from construction cost alone; access, health, housing need and long-term effects matter.

misconceptions.mistake: Defining opportunity cost as all alternatives.
misconceptions.correction: It is the value of the next-best forgone alternative.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating scarcity as the same as poverty.
misconceptions.correction: Scarcity applies whenever resources are limited relative to possible uses.

practice.prompt: Define opportunity cost and give one school-based example.
hints: Name the next-best choice given up.
solution: Opportunity cost is the next-best alternative forgone; for example, spending a free period rehearsing means giving up the next-best use of that time.

practice.prompt: Explain why clean water can be scarce in a region with high rainfall.
hints: Scarcity can involve access and infrastructure.
solution: Rainfall does not guarantee safe storage, treatment or distribution.
Pollution, seasonal variation and unequal infrastructure can limit usable supply.

practice.prompt: A school can fund either smaller classes or a new sports hall. Evaluate the decision information needed.
hints: Avoid choosing without evidence.
solution: Compare learning needs, facility condition, student access, recurring staffing costs and long-term use.
Identify affected groups and uncertainty.
Reach a conditional decision based on the strongest need and feasible costs.

practice.prompt: A school has an empty room but no available teacher hours. Why can extra lessons remain scarce?
hints: Production requires several inputs.
One unused resource does not supply all the others.
solution: The room supplies space, but teaching also requires time and staff.
Limited teacher hours still constrain lessons, so empty space does not eliminate scarcity.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical frontier allows at most 30 kits at a fixed output of 10 signs. Classify 20 kits and 10 signs, then 40 kits and 10 signs.
hints: Compare each kit count with the stated maximum.
Hold sign output fixed.
solution: 20 kits and 10 signs is feasible but below the stated maximum at that sign output.
40 kits and 10 signs is unattainable with the stated resources and technology.

checklist: I state a realistic next-best alternative.
I compare short- and long-term effects.

notes.title: Unused capacity differs from unlimited resources
paragraphs: Scarcity arises because available resources cannot satisfy every competing use. Unemployment or unused machinery does not remove scarcity: it can indicate that production is below what existing resources could achieve. A production possibility frontier represents combinations attainable with current resources and technology. Points inside may reflect idle resources or inefficient use; points beyond require changes in capacity or are currently unattainable. Moving along the frontier involves a trade-off, while moving towards it can raise output without sacrificing the other good. The model simplifies reality by holding technology and resources fixed during the comparison.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical workshop: with current resources it can produce 10 desks and 20 stools, but currently makes 6 desks and 20 stools. Interpret a move to the first combination.
steps: The stated feasible combination shows four additional desks can be made without reducing stools.
The move uses previously idle or inefficiently employed capacity rather than requiring a trade-off along the frontier.
workedExamples.conclusion: Scarcity remains because not every imaginable combination is attainable.

flashcards.front: What does scarcity require?
flashcards.back: Competing uses relative to limited resources.

flashcards.front: What can an inside-frontier point indicate?
flashcards.back: Idle resources or inefficient resource use.

flashcards.front: What does movement along a frontier involve?
flashcards.back: A trade-off between outputs.

flashcards.front: What can shift a frontier outwards?
flashcards.back: More productive resources or improved technology.

diagrams.title: Unused capacity differs from unlimited resources
diagrams.description: Better utilisation can increase output within an existing constraint.

edges.label: use idle or inefficiently employed resources

lessons.summary: Explain when private decisions create wider costs or benefits and evaluate targeted responses.
objectives: Distinguish private and external effects.
Explain over- or under-allocation.
Evaluate policy using evidence and trade-offs.
keyIdeas: Market prices may omit effects experienced by third parties.
A policy should target the mechanism causing the failure.
Government action also carries information, enforcement and equity costs.

definitions.meaning: A cost or benefit of an activity experienced by a third party and not fully reflected in the market decision.
Private cost plus external cost.
A good considered under-consumed when decisions omit wider benefits or information.

method: Identify the decision-maker and third party.
Trace the unpriced cost or benefit.
Explain the resulting quantity problem.
Compare policy impact, evidence, equity and implementation.

workedExample.prompt: Explain a congestion charge for a crowded city centre.
steps: Each driver considers fuel and time but may not bear all delay and pollution imposed on others.
A charge raises the private cost toward the social cost.
Some lower-value journeys shift time, route or transport mode.
workedExample.conclusion: The policy can reduce overuse, but evaluation requires demand responsiveness, alternatives and distributional effects.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling any undesirable outcome a market failure.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the specific mechanism, such as an externality or information gap.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming a tax removes all harmful activity.
misconceptions.correction: It changes incentives; the size of response depends on design and elasticity.

practice.prompt: Identify one negative externality from urban car use and the affected third party.
hints: Name a cost outside the driver’s decision.
solution: Air pollution can harm residents who are not part of the journey transaction.

practice.prompt: Explain why vaccination may be under-consumed in a free market.
hints: Separate private and external benefit.
solution: The vaccinated person gains private protection.
Others may gain reduced transmission risk.
If the buyer considers only private benefit, demand can be below the socially beneficial level.

practice.prompt: Evaluate a ban versus a per-unit tax on single-use bags.
hints: Compare certainty, flexibility, enforcement and equity.
solution: A ban can sharply reduce use but removes flexibility and needs exemptions or enforcement.
A tax preserves choice and raises revenue but may be too low to change behaviour.
The better instrument depends on harm, substitutes, enforcement and observed demand response.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical private marginal cost is 12 credits and marginal external cost is 5 credits per unit. Find social marginal cost and the unpriced gap.
hints: Add both components.
The gap is the external component.
solution: Social marginal cost = 12 + 5 = 17 credits per unit.
The gap between social and private cost is 5 credits per unit.

practice.prompt: A garden provides enjoyment to nearby residents who do not pay its owner. Identify the possible externality and one limitation of inferring under-provision.
hints: The effect benefits third parties.
The size of the benefit and private incentives are unspecified.
solution: This may be a positive consumption externality because neighbours receive an unpaid benefit.
Under-provision is a model possibility, but its extent requires evidence on marginal benefits, costs and existing incentives.

checklist: I distinguish private and social effects.

notes.title: An unpriced cost separates private and social cost
paragraphs: An externality occurs when a decision affects third parties and that effect is not fully reflected in the decision-maker’s costs or benefits. A negative production externality makes social marginal cost exceed private marginal cost in the basic model. Private buyers and sellers may then choose more output than the socially efficient quantity. A corrective policy needs evidence about the external effect, behaviour and implementation costs. Not every inconvenience is an externality, and not every intervention improves welfare. The analysis should identify the third party, the unpriced effect and the mechanism through which a policy changes incentives.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical production: private marginal cost is 8 credits per item and external damage is 3 credits per item. Find social marginal cost and interpret a 3-credit corrective charge.
steps: Social marginal cost = 8 + 3 = 11 credits per item.
A 3-credit charge would make the producer face the modelled external cost if the estimate and implementation are accurate.
workedExamples.conclusion: The calculation illustrates an incentive correction, not proof that the real damage is known exactly.

flashcards.front: Who is a third party?
flashcards.back: Someone affected who is not one of the immediate parties to the transaction.

flashcards.front: How is social marginal cost formed here?
flashcards.back: Private marginal cost plus marginal external cost.

flashcards.front: What does a corrective charge aim to do?
flashcards.back: Make decision-makers face an otherwise external cost.

flashcards.front: Why can policy evaluation remain uncertain?
flashcards.back: Damage estimates, behavioural responses and enforcement costs may be uncertain.

diagrams.title: An unpriced cost separates private and social cost
diagrams.description: The external damage adds to the resource cost faced privately.

lessons.summary: Identify the next-best alternative forgone and calculate trade-offs under an explicit resource constraint.
objectives: Distinguish opportunity cost from total spending.
Calculate a trade-off in units of another good.
Recognise that the best alternative depends on the decision-maker.
explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best feasible alternative given up when a choice uses a scarce resource. It is not the sum of every possible alternative. A monetary payment can help measure a trade-off, but time and other resources also have alternative uses. State the actual choice and the best rejected option before evaluating whether the choice was worthwhile. A cost already incurred and unrecoverable is a sunk cost; it does not change the alternatives available now.

A simple budget model makes the trade-off explicit. With a fixed budget and constant prices, buying more of one good leaves less money for another. Divide the price of the chosen good by the price of the alternative to express its cost in alternative units. This calculation describes affordability, not preferences or social value. Every number below is hypothetical; the examples do not report an actual school budget or prescribe a spending decision.
keyIdeas: Use the next-best feasible alternative.
Trade-offs need units and constraints.
Affordability does not establish desirability.

definitions.meaning: The value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone.
The combinations affordable with a specified budget and prices.
An already incurred cost that cannot be recovered by the current decision.

method: Identify the limited resource and feasible options.
State the next-best rejected option.
Calculate the trade-off using consistent units.
Separate the constraint from a judgement of value.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical case: a club has 36 credits. Posters cost 6 credits each and leaflets 2 credits each, at constant prices. Calculate the leaflet opportunity cost of one extra poster when the whole budget is spent.
steps: One poster uses 6 credits that could buy 6/2 = 3 leaflets.
The budget could fund 6 posters alone or 18 leaflets alone.
At a feasible mixed combination, one extra poster requires three fewer leaflets if the full budget stays fixed.
workedExample.conclusion: The opportunity cost is 3 leaflets per poster in this two-good budget model. The calculation does not decide which publicity option is better.

misconceptions.mistake: Adding every rejected option together.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the best feasible alternative instead.

misconceptions.mistake: Keeping an option because unrecoverable money was already spent.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the remaining costs and benefits of the current alternatives.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: a notebook costs 8 credits and a pen 2 credits. With a fully spent fixed budget and constant prices, calculate the pen opportunity cost of one extra notebook.
hints: Use the ratio of prices.
solution: 8/2 = 4 pens per notebook.
Buying the extra notebook requires giving up four pens in this two-good model.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical production frontier: moving from 6 kits and 10 signs to 4 kits and 16 signs uses the same resources efficiently. Find the average kit opportunity cost of each additional sign over this move.
hints: Compare changes, not totals.
solution: The move gains 16 - 10 = 6 signs and gives up 6 - 4 = 2 kits.
Average opportunity cost = 2/6 = 1/3 kit per additional sign over this interval.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: a non-refundable workshop ticket is already paid for. A learner can attend or use the same time to prepare for an assessment. Explain how opportunity cost should guide the current choice.
hints: The ticket payment cannot be recovered by either choice.
solution: The ticket price is sunk for the current decision.
Compare the remaining benefit of attendance with the best alternative use of the time and any new costs.
If assessment preparation is the next-best feasible option, its forgone value is the time opportunity cost of attending.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical learner can spend one hour reading, practising piano or resting, in that preference order. If reading is chosen, identify the opportunity cost.
hints: Choose the next-best feasible activity.
Do not combine every alternative.
solution: The opportunity cost is the benefit of practising piano.
Rest is a lower-ranked alternative and is not added to the next-best forgone option.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical workshop can trade off 3 shelves for 2 desks along a linear frontier. Find the shelf opportunity cost of 5 extra desks.
hints: Find shelves per desk.
Apply the constant ratio.
solution: Each desk costs 3/2 = 1.5 shelves.
Five extra desks cost 5 × 1.5 = 7.5 shelf-equivalents in the divisible-output model.

checklist: I exclude unrecoverable costs from current trade-offs.

notes.title: A ranked choice identifies one forgone alternative
paragraphs: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone. It is not automatically the sum of every rejected option, and it need not be a monetary payment. Time spent on one activity excludes another use of that time even when the chosen activity is free. A decision can involve several constraints, so identify which alternative is genuinely feasible. Past costs that cannot be recovered do not change the current trade-off, although future costs and benefits do. Compare the alternatives at the decision point and make the relevant resource constraint explicit.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical learner has two free hours and ranks feasible options: music rehearsal first, sport second, and a film third. What is the opportunity cost of choosing rehearsal?
steps: The next-best feasible alternative is sport.
The opportunity cost is the benefit of the forgone sport session, not sport plus the film.
workedExamples.conclusion: No ticket price is needed for a time-based opportunity cost.

flashcards.front: Which alternative defines opportunity cost?
flashcards.back: The next-best feasible one forgone.

flashcards.front: Can a free activity have opportunity cost?
flashcards.back: Yes; it uses scarce time or other resources.

flashcards.front: Should all rejected alternatives be added?
flashcards.back: No.

flashcards.front: Do irrecoverable past costs determine the current trade-off?
flashcards.back: No; current feasible alternatives and future consequences matter.

diagrams.title: A ranked choice identifies one forgone alternative
diagrams.description: The best rejected feasible option defines the relevant trade-off.

lessons.summary: Compare how allocation decisions use prices, public decisions and other institutions without treating real economies as pure types.
objectives: Identify who makes allocation decisions.
Compare incentives and access under different rules.
Evaluate a mixed arrangement using stated objectives.
explanation: Economic systems organise what is produced, how resources are used and who receives output. Market allocation relies heavily on prices and decentralised decisions. Planned allocation gives public decision-makers a larger direct role in targets and distribution. These are simplifying models, not labels that fully describe every institution in a real country. Households, communities, firms and governments can use different arrangements within the same economy.

Evaluate an arrangement against a clear objective such as access, responsiveness or efficient use of resources. Prices can communicate willingness and ability to pay, which need not match need. Public provision can broaden access but still faces scarcity, information limits and funding choices. A free service has resource costs even when the user pays no fee. Specify the rules and available evidence instead of assuming that ownership alone guarantees efficiency, fairness or a particular outcome.
keyIdeas: Allocation rules shape incentives and access.
Most arrangements combine institutions.
A zero user price does not mean zero resource cost.

definitions.meaning: Allocation influenced by prices and decentralised exchange.
Allocation substantially directed through collective or public decisions.
An economy combining market mechanisms with public and other forms of allocation.

method: Identify the resource and allocation rule.
Name who decides and who can access the output.
Compare incentives, information and funding constraints.
Judge against stated objectives with appropriate evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical case: a publicly funded library offers free entry while a private café inside sells drinks at posted prices. Explain why one allocation label is insufficient.
steps: Library access is funded collectively and is not conditional on paying an entry price.
Café drinks are allocated through purchases at prices.
Both activities still use scarce staff time and space, and their performance needs separate evidence.
workedExample.conclusion: The arrangement combines public access provision with market exchange. Neither ownership nor a free entrance establishes that all users’ needs are met.

misconceptions.mistake: Equating a market price with social need.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish purchasing power from need and external effects.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming free provision uses no scarce resources.
misconceptions.correction: Identify staffing, materials, facilities and funding trade-offs.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: households buy bread from competing shops, while a council allocates emergency shelter places using need criteria. Identify the two allocation rules.
hints: Compare purchase with administrative criteria.
solution: Bread is allocated through market purchases.
Shelter places are allocated through a public decision rule based on assessed need.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: a free community pool becomes crowded. Explain why scarcity persists without an entry fee.
hints: Consider capacity and time.
solution: Pool space and staff capacity are limited even when users pay no fee.
Excess demand may require booking, queues or another allocation rule.
A zero price to the user does not eliminate the resources needed to operate the service.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: a town debates private or public operation of a bus route. Propose evidence for comparing access and efficiency without assuming one owner type must win.
hints: Use the same objectives for both options.
solution: Compare coverage, fares and accessibility for different users to assess access.
Compare reliable service output with operating and capital resources to assess efficiency.
Consider contract rules, accountability and funding; ownership alone does not determine the observed outcomes.

practice.prompt: A free exhibition admits visitors in booking order until full. Identify the allocation mechanism and one possible access limitation.
hints: The order of reservations decides places.
Consider access to the booking process.
solution: Places are allocated by booking order rather than an admission price.
People lacking timely booking access may be excluded even though entry is free.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical public museum charges entry while a private charity offers free classes. Why cannot ownership alone identify the allocation rule?
hints: Public does not necessarily mean free.
Private does not necessarily mean price allocation.
solution: The museum combines public ownership with a monetary entry charge.
The charity combines private organisation with free provision, so price and eligibility rules must be examined separately from ownership.

checklist: I separate need and purchasing power.

notes.title: Zero price still requires allocation
paragraphs: Economic systems use different institutions to decide what to produce, how to produce it and who receives the output. Prices, administrative rules, queues and household decisions can all allocate scarce resources. A zero monetary price does not remove allocation: capacity may be rationed through waiting, eligibility or availability. Ownership and allocation should be analysed separately, since a publicly owned service can charge a fee and a private organisation can provide free access. Evaluate outcomes using specified criteria such as efficiency, equity, responsiveness and access, recognising that one allocation rule may improve one criterion while worsening another.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical free sports facility has 20 places and 35 applicants. Compare first-come allocation with a needs-based rule.
steps: First-come allocation uses arrival order and may favour people able to queue early.
A needs-based rule uses eligibility criteria but requires information and administration.
workedExamples.conclusion: Both ration the same scarce places despite a zero entry price.

flashcards.front: Does zero price remove scarcity?
flashcards.back: No; capacity may still be limited.

flashcards.front: Name a non-price allocation rule.
flashcards.back: Queuing, eligibility criteria or a lottery.

flashcards.front: Is ownership identical to allocation method?
flashcards.back: No; each should be identified separately.

flashcards.front: What should a comparison of systems specify?
flashcards.back: The outcomes and criteria used to judge them.

diagrams.title: Zero price still requires allocation
diagrams.description: Limited capacity is rationed by a rule even without a fee.

nodes.label: Allocation rule
nodes.detail: Queue, criteria or lottery determines access

lessons.summary: Use a supply schedule to distinguish price-driven movements from shifts caused by production conditions.
objectives: Calculate quantity supplied in a stated model.
Distinguish a movement along supply from a shift.
Explain the role of production costs and time horizon.
explanation: Supply describes the quantities sellers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a stated period. In a basic competitive model, a higher output price can make additional production worthwhile, holding other conditions constant. A change in that good’s price moves along an existing supply curve. A change in input costs, technology or the number of sellers can instead alter quantities offered at each price and shift the curve.

Always identify the product, units and period. A schedule of units per week cannot be compared directly with a monthly schedule. A model equation is valid only over its stated range; a negative quantity outside that range is not a meaningful prediction. Supply response also depends on adjustment time and capacity. Explain the mechanism before choosing a direction, and avoid treating more observed sales as proof of a supply shift when demand may also have changed.
keyIdeas: Own-price changes create movements along a given curve.
Production conditions can shift supply.
Quantity needs units, period and model range.

definitions.meaning: The amount offered at a particular price during a specified period.
A change in the quantities offered at given prices.
Holding other relevant conditions constant in a model comparison.

method: Read price and quantity units and the valid range.
Identify whether own price or another condition changed.
Calculate or describe the resulting quantity relation.
State assumptions and avoid inferring a cause from quantity alone.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical weekly supply model: Qs = 4P - 8, where P is credits per item and Qs items per week, valid for P from 2 to 8. Compare supply at P = 5 and P = 6 with other conditions unchanged.
steps: At P = 5, Qs = 4 × 5 - 8 = 12 items per week.
At P = 6, Qs = 4 × 6 - 8 = 16 items per week.
The rise of 4 items per week is a movement along the same supply relation caused by own price.
workedExample.conclusion: Quantity supplied increases from 12 to 16 items per week. The equation itself has not shifted.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling every quantity increase an increase in supply.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish a movement along the relation from a change in the relation.

misconceptions.mistake: Extrapolating a linear equation to negative quantities.
misconceptions.correction: Respect the stated range and physical meaning.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical model: Qs = 3P - 6 items per week, valid for prices from 2 to 10 credits. Find quantity supplied at P = 7.
hints: Substitute within the valid range.
solution: Qs = 3 × 7 - 6 = 15 items per week.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: a bakery’s flour becomes cheaper while its bread price is unchanged. Explain the likely supply effect in a basic competitive model.
hints: Compare production costs at the same output price.
solution: Lower flour costs can make supplying additional bread worthwhile at the same bread price.
Supply shifts to the right, holding other relevant conditions constant.
This is not a movement caused by a change in bread’s own price.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: weekly sales rise from 40 to 55 units. No price or cost information is supplied. Evaluate “supply must have increased”.
hints: Observed sales reflect both sides of a market.
solution: Higher sales alone do not identify the changed relation.
Demand could have increased, supply could have increased, or both could have changed.
Obtain price, cost and demand-condition evidence before identifying the mechanism.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical supply is Qs = 2Ps + 4, where Ps is the seller’s receipt. Buyers pay 9 credits and a 3-credit seller tax applies. Find Qs.
hints: Find the net receipt first.
Substitute into the supplied relation.
solution: Ps = 9 − 3 = 6 credits.
Qs = 2 × 6 + 4 = 16 units per period.

practice.prompt: A new machine reduces the cost of producing each item while the item’s market price is unchanged. Distinguish the supply effect from a movement along the old curve.
hints: A non-price determinant changed.
Compare quantities at the same price.
solution: Lower production costs allow greater quantity supplied at a given price in the basic model.
This is a rightward supply shift, not movement caused by the item’s own price on the old curve.

notes.title: A tax separates buyer and seller prices
paragraphs: Supply describes quantities producers are willing and able to offer at different prices over a specified period, holding other relevant conditions constant. A change in the product’s own price causes movement along a supply curve. A change in production costs, technology or the number of sellers can shift the curve. For a per-unit tax on sellers, the price received after tax matters for their supply decision. A simple linear model can represent this by subtracting the tax from the buyer’s price. The result depends on the specified model and does not by itself identify how the tax burden is shared.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical supply is Qs = 5P, with P the price received by sellers. Buyers pay 6 credits, but sellers remit a 2-credit tax per item. Find supply.
steps: Sellers retain 6 − 2 = 4 credits per item.
Qs = 5 × 4 = 20 items per period.
workedExamples.conclusion: Using the full buyer price would incorrectly ignore the tax wedge.

flashcards.front: What causes movement along a supply curve?
flashcards.back: A change in the product’s own price, other conditions fixed.

flashcards.front: Name a supply shifter.
flashcards.back: Input costs, technology or number of sellers.

flashcards.front: Which price matters in the stated taxed supply model?
flashcards.back: The price sellers retain after the per-unit tax.

flashcards.front: Does lower cost generally shift supply rightwards?
flashcards.back: Yes in the basic model, with other conditions unchanged.

diagrams.title: A tax separates buyer and seller prices
diagrams.description: Supply responds to the price retained in the stated model.

edges.label: apply the supply function to the net price

lessons.summary: Use demand and supply together to identify equilibrium and distinguish demand shifts from price-driven movements.
objectives: Calculate quantity demanded at a stated price.
Solve a simple market equilibrium.
Distinguish desire, effective demand and a demand shift.
explanation: Demand relates quantities buyers are willing and able to buy to a good’s price over a specified period. Desire alone is not effective demand because ability to pay also matters. In the basic model, a change in own price moves along the demand curve when other conditions are held fixed. Income, preferences, related-good prices or the number of buyers can shift the relationship. For a normal good, higher income increases demand; that direction is not universal for every good.

Equilibrium in the simple competitive market occurs where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. It is a model of compatible buying and selling plans, not a guarantee of fairness or social efficiency. At another price, compare the two quantities to identify excess demand or excess supply. Keep the same good, time period and units throughout. A price and quantity observation alone may not reveal which underlying curve shifted.
keyIdeas: Demand includes willingness and ability to pay.
A demand shift changes quantities at given prices.
Equilibrium matches planned quantities.

definitions.meaning: The amount buyers are willing and able to buy at a specified price and time period.
A good for which demand rises as income rises, holding other conditions fixed.
A model outcome where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

method: Identify the good, price and quantity units.
Distinguish own-price movements from changed demand conditions.
Set demand equal to supply when finding equilibrium.
Interpret the result and state the model’s limits.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical market: Qd = 80 - 5P and Qs = 10 + 5P, in items per week, with P in credits per item. Both relations apply from P = 0 to 10. Find equilibrium.
steps: Then 70 = 10P, so P = 7 credits per item.
At P = 7, both quantities equal 45 items per week.
workedExample.conclusion: The model equilibrium is P = 7 and Q = 45 per week. Matching plans does not establish a fair distribution or include unpriced effects.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating desire without purchasing capacity as effective demand.
misconceptions.correction: State both willingness and ability to buy.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a lower price an outward demand shift.
misconceptions.correction: A lower own price moves along the curve when other conditions are fixed.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical demand: Qd = 60 - 4P items per week for P from 0 to 12 credits. Find Qd at P = 8.
hints: Substitute the price.
solution: Qd = 60 - 4 × 8 = 28 items per week.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical market: Qd = 100 - 10P and Qs = 20 + 10P, valid for P from 0 to 10 credits, quantities per day. Find equilibrium price and quantity.
hints: Set the planned quantities equal.
solution: 100 - 10P = 20 + 10P, so 80 = 20P and P = 4 credits.
Q = 100 - 40 = 60 items per day; supply also gives 20 + 40 = 60.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: incomes rise and a product is specified to be a normal good. Explain the demand effect and why the final quantity change cannot be found without supply information.
hints: Separate the demand shift from the new intersection.
solution: Demand shifts right because buyers demand more at given prices.
The new equilibrium depends on the supply relationship and other unchanged conditions.
The statement alone provides no numerical size for the quantity or price change.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical printers and compatible ink are complements. Ink prices rise while printer prices are unchanged. Predict printer demand in the basic model.
hints: The cost of using a printer rises.
This is not a change in the printer’s own price.
solution: Higher ink prices raise the cost of using the combined products.
Printer demand may shift leftwards, with fewer printers demanded at each unchanged printer price.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical demand shifts from Qd = 50 − 2P to Qd = 62 − 2P. At P = 6, calculate both quantities and the shift in quantity demanded at that price.
hints: Substitute the same price into both relations.
Subtract the original quantity.
solution: Original quantity = 38; new quantity = 50.
At the same price, quantity demanded increases by 12 units per period.

checklist: I check both sides at equilibrium.

notes.title: A substitute-price change shifts demand
paragraphs: Demand depends on willingness and ability to purchase over a specified period. A product’s own-price change creates a movement along its demand curve when other conditions are fixed. Prices of related goods can shift demand: a rise in a substitute’s price can increase demand for the product, while a rise in a complement’s price can reduce it. These relationships depend on actual consumer use rather than the labels alone. Distinguish demand from the quantity purchased after market adjustment, because the final price and quantity also depend on supply and any capacity constraints.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical commuters treat buses and trains as substitutes. Train fares rise while bus fares initially stay fixed. Explain the likely bus-demand effect.
steps: Some commuters may switch towards buses because trains become relatively more expensive.
Bus demand shifts rightwards in the stated substitute model.
workedExamples.conclusion: The eventual bus fare and passenger quantity also depend on bus supply and capacity.

flashcards.front: What is a substitute?
flashcards.back: A good or service that can replace another in use.

flashcards.front: What is a complement?
flashcards.back: A good or service used together with another.

flashcards.front: What changes demand when a related good’s price changes?
flashcards.back: The demand curve may shift.

flashcards.front: Does demand alone determine final market quantity?
flashcards.back: No; supply also matters.

diagrams.title: A substitute-price change shifts demand
diagrams.description: Relative cost alters consumers’ choices between services.

nodes.label: Bus demand rises
nodes.detail: More bus journeys demanded at a given fare

lessons.summary: Calculate percentage responsiveness using a stated convention and connect it to revenue without confusing revenue and profit.
objectives: Calculate midpoint price elasticity of demand.
Interpret elastic, inelastic and unit-elastic values.
Explain revenue changes under a stated demand relation.
explanation: Elasticity compares percentage changes, so it has no physical unit. For price elasticity of demand, divide percentage change in quantity demanded by percentage change in price, holding other demand conditions fixed. Here use the midpoint method: divide each change by the average of its initial and final values. The signed demand elasticity is usually negative in the basic model; compare its absolute magnitude with one to describe responsiveness. Supply elasticity uses quantity supplied instead.

A magnitude above one is elastic, below one inelastic and equal to one unit elastic. Do not confuse elasticity with a curve’s numerical slope, which depends on units. Total revenue equals price multiplied by quantity sold; profit also subtracts costs. Elastic demand over an interval can make revenue fall when price rises, but a pair of observed points affected by other changes does not identify a causal elasticity. State the interval and convention, and keep precision until the final answer.
keyIdeas: Percentage responsiveness is unitless.
The midpoint convention must be explicit.
Revenue and profit are different.

definitions.meaning: The change divided by the average of the starting and ending values, multiplied by 100.
Percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in own price with other demand conditions fixed.
Price multiplied by quantity sold over the specified period.

method: Calculate the price and quantity averages.
Divide each change by its average.
Take the ratio and classify its absolute magnitude.
Check revenue and state assumptions about other conditions.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical movement along one demand curve: price rises from 4 to 6 credits and weekly quantity falls from 60 to 40. Use midpoint elasticity and compare revenue.
steps: Quantity change = -20/50 = -0.4, or -40%; price change = 2/5 = 0.4, or 40%.
Signed elasticity = -40/40 = -1; its magnitude is 1, so demand is unit elastic over this interval.
Revenue is 4 × 60 = 240 credits before and 6 × 40 = 240 credits after.
workedExample.conclusion: Revenue is unchanged in this interval. Costs are not supplied, so the example does not establish a profit change.

misconceptions.mistake: Using the initial base for one change and the midpoint for the other.
misconceptions.correction: Apply the same stated convention consistently.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a negative elasticity less than one and therefore inelastic.
misconceptions.correction: Classify demand responsiveness using the absolute magnitude.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical fixed demand relation: price rises from 10 to 12 credits and quantity falls from 110 to 90 units per week. Use the midpoint method to calculate signed elasticity and classify its magnitude.
hints: Use average quantity 100 and average price 11.
solution: Quantity change = -20/100 = -0.2; price change = 2/11.
Elasticity = -0.2 ÷ (2/11) = -1.1; magnitude 1.1 is elastic.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical demand: price rises from 5 to 6 credits and weekly quantity falls from 100 to 80. Calculate revenue before and after, the revenue change, and explain why profit cannot be determined.
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
solution: Before: 5 × 100 = 500 credits; after: 6 × 80 = 480 credits.
Revenue change = -20 credits, a 4% decrease relative to the initial 500.
Profit cannot be found without relevant cost data.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical case: price and sales both rise after a major advertising campaign. Evaluate using those two observations alone to estimate demand’s own-price elasticity.
hints: Did demand conditions remain fixed?
solution: The campaign may have shifted demand, so the points need not lie on one unchanged demand curve.
The observed ratio mixes price movement with changed demand conditions.
It cannot by itself identify the causal own-price responsiveness; additional evidence or an appropriate design is needed.

practice.prompt: Using initial-value percentages, income rises 10% while demand for a good falls 5%, other influences fixed. Find income elasticity and classify the good.
hints: Retain the negative sign.
Classification follows the sign.
solution: Income elasticity = −5/10 = −0.5.
The good is inferior over the supplied range, which does not describe its physical quality.

practice.prompt: Income and sales both rise during a price discount. Can the sales change alone estimate income elasticity?
hints: Two demand influences changed.
Separate income from the price response.
solution: The discount can increase quantity demanded independently of income.
The observation confounds income and price effects; hold price fixed or use a method that separates their contributions.

checklist: I separate revenue, profit and causal evidence.

notes.title: Income elasticity compares proportional changes
paragraphs: Elasticity measures proportional responsiveness rather than the slope alone. Income elasticity of demand compares the percentage change in quantity demanded with the percentage change in income, holding other relevant influences fixed. A positive value indicates a normal good in the model; a negative value indicates an inferior good over the stated range. These are descriptions of demand responses, not judgements about quality. State the percentage-change convention because initial-value and midpoint calculations can differ. An observed association does not isolate income responsiveness if prices, tastes or availability also change during the comparison.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical income rises from 100 to 120 credits while quantity demanded rises from 50 to 55 units, other influences fixed. Use initial-value percentages to find income elasticity.
steps: Income rises 20/100 = 20%; quantity rises 5/50 = 10%.
Income elasticity = 10%/20% = 0.5.
workedExamples.conclusion: The positive value classifies the good as normal over this range.

flashcards.front: What is income elasticity?
flashcards.back: Percentage quantity-demand change divided by percentage income change.

flashcards.front: What does negative income elasticity indicate?
flashcards.back: An inferior good over the stated range.

flashcards.front: Does inferior mean poor quality?
flashcards.back: No; it describes the demand response to income.

flashcards.front: Why name the percentage convention?
flashcards.back: Different denominators can produce different numerical estimates.

diagrams.title: Income elasticity compares proportional changes
diagrams.description: The ratio uses percentage changes rather than raw units.

edges.label: divide proportional quantity change by income change

lessons.summary: Analyse price controls and policy trade-offs using explicit model assumptions and distributional evidence.
objectives: Identify whether a price control is binding.
Calculate excess demand or supply in a simple model.
Evaluate policy effects without equating a model prediction with a universal outcome.
explanation: Governments can influence allocation through taxes, subsidies, regulation and provision. Identify the problem and the mechanism a policy targets before judging it. A price ceiling sets a maximum price; a price floor sets a minimum. In a basic competitive model, a ceiling below the uncontrolled equilibrium is binding and creates excess demand at that price. A floor above equilibrium creates excess supply. Controls on the other side may leave the equilibrium unchanged.

Compare planned quantities rather than assuming every intended purchase occurs. A shortage measures excess demand at the controlled price; it is not the number of successful trades. Allocation rules, enforcement and changes in quality can matter. A per-unit tax creates a gap between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive, but who formally remits it does not alone determine who bears its burden. Evaluate responses using elasticity, available alternatives, administrative costs and effects on different groups.
keyIdeas: Compare a control with the uncontrolled equilibrium.
Shortage describes incompatible plans at a price.
Policy incidence and distribution require evidence.

definitions.meaning: A maximum price below the uncontrolled equilibrium in the stated competitive model.
Quantity demanded minus quantity supplied at a given price when demand exceeds supply.
How a tax’s economic burden is distributed among affected parties.

method: State the objective and market assumptions.
Find the uncontrolled comparison outcome.
Calculate quantities at the policy price or explain its mechanism.
Evaluate allocation, distribution and implementation limits.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical competitive market: Qd = 100 - 10P and Qs = 20 + 10P, units per day, valid from P = 0 to 10 credits. A ceiling sets P no higher than 3. Find the model shortage at the ceiling.
steps: Uncontrolled equilibrium is P = 4, Q = 60, so a ceiling of 3 is binding.
At P = 3, Qd = 70 and Qs = 50.
Shortage = 70 - 50 = 20 units per day; without extra supply, at most 50 units could be traded under these plans.
workedExample.conclusion: The lower permitted price leaves 20 units of excess demand at that price. Which buyers obtain the available units depends on allocation, not demand alone.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming every maximum price changes the market.
misconceptions.correction: Compare it with the uncontrolled equilibrium.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming the party paying the tax to government bears all of it.
misconceptions.correction: Examine how buyer and seller prices change.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical market at a binding price ceiling: buyers demand 90 units per week and sellers offer 65. Calculate the shortage.
hints: Subtract quantity supplied from quantity demanded.
solution: Shortage = 90 - 65 = 25 units per week.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical market equilibrium price is 8 credits. A price ceiling is 10 credits. With all other conditions unchanged and no additional rules, explain whether it is binding.
hints: Can the old equilibrium price still occur legally?
solution: The equilibrium price of 8 is below the maximum of 10.
The ceiling is non-binding in this model, so the old equilibrium remains permitted.
A shortage cannot be inferred merely from the existence of this ceiling.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical proposal: subsidise bus fares to reduce car congestion. Identify a possible mechanism, a limitation and evidence for evaluation.
hints: Will riders switch from cars or from other modes?
solution: A lower fare may induce some car users to switch to buses if routes and capacity are suitable.
Some extra bus journeys may replace walking or be newly generated, and the subsidy requires funding.
Examine mode switching, congestion, service capacity and distribution of benefits before judging effectiveness.

practice.prompt: At a hypothetical binding floor, sellers offer 120 units and buyers demand 85. Find the surplus and maximum private-market sales if no public buyer exists.
hints: Subtract demand from supply.
Private buyers limit sales at that price.
solution: Surplus = 120 − 85 = 35 units.
At most 85 units are sold to those private buyers under the stated model.
successCriteria: Does not equate supply with sales.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical equilibrium price is 12 credits and a price floor is 9 credits. Is it binding, with all other conditions unchanged?
hints: The equilibrium is already above the minimum.
Check whether the legal constraint changes the chosen price.
solution: The floor is non-binding because 12 exceeds the 9-credit minimum.
The model equilibrium price and quantity remain unchanged.

checklist: I check whether the rule binds.

notes.title: A binding floor separates supply and demand
paragraphs: A price floor prevents legal prices from falling below a stated level. It is binding only when set above the otherwise prevailing equilibrium price in the basic competitive model. At a binding floor, quantity supplied may exceed quantity demanded, creating a surplus. The quantity actually traded depends on additional rules, such as whether a public buyer purchases excess supply. A non-binding floor does not change the model equilibrium. Policy evaluation should distinguish intended benefits to sellers from consequences for buyers, unsold output and administration, and should state the assumptions behind the predicted quantities.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical market: Qd = 60 − 5P and Qs = 10 + 5P. A floor sets P = 7. Find equilibrium and the surplus at the floor.
steps: Equilibrium: 60 − 5P = 10 + 5P gives P = 5 and Q = 35.
At P = 7, Qd = 25 and Qs = 45, giving a surplus of 20.
workedExamples.conclusion: The floor is binding; offered supply is not automatically all sold.

flashcards.front: When is a price floor binding?
flashcards.back: When it exceeds the otherwise equilibrium price.

flashcards.front: What is a surplus?
flashcards.back: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded at the stated price.

flashcards.front: Does offered quantity equal sales automatically?
flashcards.back: No; buyers or additional purchasing rules determine sales.

flashcards.front: What happens to a non-binding floor in the basic model?
flashcards.back: The equilibrium remains unchanged.

diagrams.title: A binding floor separates supply and demand
diagrams.description: A higher legal price can create unsold offered output.

lessons.summary: Interpret labour-market measures and distinguish nominal pay, purchasing power and model-dependent employment effects.
objectives: Identify labour demand and supply correctly.
Calculate unemployment and real-wage changes.
Evaluate wage-policy claims with stated assumptions.
explanation: In a labour market, workers supply labour and employers demand it. Demand for workers depends partly on demand for the output they help produce, as well as productivity, technology and costs. A wage is the price of labour over a stated unit of time. The basic competitive model is useful for tracing incentives, but actual employment outcomes can also depend on employer market power, bargaining, institutions and adjustment time.

The unemployment rate compares unemployed people with the labour force, not the entire population. For these exercises, the labour force consists of employed people plus those without work who are available and actively seeking it. Real wages measure purchasing power: divide a nominal-wage index by a price index, using a common base. A higher money wage need not buy more if prices rise faster. State definitions and periods before comparing rates or drawing conclusions about living standards.
keyIdeas: Workers supply and employers demand labour.
Use the labour force as the unemployment denominator.
Real pay adjusts nominal pay for prices.

definitions.meaning: Employed people plus unemployed people under the stated availability and job-search definition.
Unemployed people divided by the labour force, multiplied by 100.
A wage expressed in purchasing-power terms after adjusting for a relevant price measure.

method: Read the population, labour definition and period.
Identify the appropriate numerator and denominator.
Calculate rates or real-wage ratios consistently.
Qualify employment or welfare claims using the model and omitted factors.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical economy: 900 employed people, 100 unemployed people meeting the stated definition, and 200 people outside the labour force. Calculate the unemployment rate.
steps: Labour force = 900 + 100 = 1,000 people.
Unemployment rate = 100/1,000 × 100 = 10%.
The 200 outside the labour force are not included in this rate’s denominator.
workedExample.conclusion: The rate is 10% of the labour force. It is not 100 divided by the entire population listed.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating every person without a job as unemployed in the rate.
misconceptions.correction: Use the specified availability and active-search criteria.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming higher nominal pay always raises purchasing power.
misconceptions.correction: Adjust for price changes over the same period.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical data: 760 employed and 40 unemployed people in the labour force. Calculate the unemployment rate.
hints: First find the labour-force total.
solution: Labour force = 760 + 40 = 800.
Unemployment rate = 40/800 × 100 = 5%.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical same-base indices rise from 100 to 104 for nominal wages and from 100 to 108 for prices. Find the final real-wage index and its percentage change from the base, to two decimal places.
hints: Real index = nominal index divided by price index times 100.
solution: Change from the base index 100 is approximately -3.70%.
Money pay rises, but measured purchasing power falls.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical claim: every increase in a minimum wage must reduce employment by the same amount. Evaluate it.
hints: A model prediction depends on the starting situation and institutions.
solution: In a basic competitive model, a binding floor can reduce labour demanded, with the size depending on responsiveness.
A non-binding change need not alter the equilibrium; employer power, bargaining and adjustment also affect actual outcomes.
The universal same-amount claim needs evidence and cannot follow from the policy label alone.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical team makes 500 units in 125 worker-hours. Find productivity and output expected from 150 hours at the same rate.
hints: Find units per hour first.
Then multiply by the new hours.
solution: Productivity = 500/125 = 4 units per worker-hour.
At the same rate, 150 hours produce 600 units.

practice.prompt: After training, output per hour rises, but a new machine is installed at the same time. Can the full increase be attributed to training?
hints: Two influences changed together.
A comparison must separate their effects.
solution: The machine may also raise output per hour, so the changes are confounded.
Use an appropriate comparison of training with similar equipment conditions before attributing the full increase to training.

notes.title: Hours and productivity jointly determine output
paragraphs: Labour productivity measures output per unit of labour input, commonly per worker-hour. It differs from total output: a firm can produce more simply by using more hours without improving productivity. Comparisons need consistent output definitions and quality. Training, equipment and organisation may affect productivity, but a before-and-after increase alone cannot identify which factor caused it. Employment statistics also require a defined population and period. People outside the labour force are not automatically counted as unemployed. Distinguishing these measures helps avoid turning a change in one indicator into an unsupported claim about all labour-market outcomes.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical workshop produces 240 items using 80 worker-hours, then 330 items using 100 worker-hours. Compare productivity.
steps: Initial productivity = 240/80 = 3 items per worker-hour.
Later productivity = 330/100 = 3.3, an increase of 0.3/3 × 100% = 10%.
workedExamples.conclusion: Total output rises 37.5%, but productivity rises only 10%.

flashcards.front: What is labour productivity?
flashcards.back: Output per unit of labour input.

flashcards.front: Can output rise without productivity rising?
flashcards.back: Yes, by using more labour hours.

flashcards.front: Why compare output quality?
flashcards.back: More low-quality units may not represent equivalent output.

flashcards.front: Are all non-employed people unemployed?
flashcards.back: No; some are outside the defined labour force.

diagrams.title: Hours and productivity jointly determine output
diagrams.description: Separate the amount of labour used from output per hour.

edges.label: calculate change from the initial productivity

lessons.summary: Compare material output and human outcomes using suitable indicators, averages and distributional limits.
objectives: Distinguish economic growth from broader development.
Calculate a per-person measure without treating it as a distribution.
Explain the scope and limits of a composite indicator.
explanation: Economic growth concerns increases in real output; development concerns broader changes in people’s opportunities and living conditions. A per-person output measure divides a total by population, but does not describe how income or services are distributed. Compare health, education, access and environmental conditions alongside economic resources. Use matched dates and definitions, and distinguish a measured indicator from the wider idea it is intended to represent.

The Human Development Index combines dimensions of health, education and income into a summary measure. It can broaden discussion beyond output alone, but an average composite does not fully describe inequality or every aspect of wellbeing. This lesson uses hypothetical arithmetic, not actual country statistics or a reconstruction of the HDI formula. For a real comparison, use the published methodology and data provenance, then examine differences within each place before making claims about all residents.
keyIdeas: Growth and development are related but distinct.
Per-person averages do not reveal distribution.
Composite indices simplify a wider picture.

definitions.meaning: An increase in real output over a specified period.
Per person, calculated by dividing a total by population.
A measure combining several indicators under a stated method.

method: Define the development question and relevant dimensions.
Check dates, units and comparability.
Calculate a suitable rate or average.
Evaluate distribution, omitted dimensions and data quality.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical region: annual real output is 240 million constant-price credits and population is 60,000. Calculate output per person and state a limitation.
steps: Output per person = 4,000 constant-price credits per year.
This is an average of output, not evidence that each resident earns or receives 4,000 credits.
workedExample.conclusion: The measure helps compare the scale of real output per person. It needs distributional and non-income indicators for a broader development judgement.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling higher total output proof of higher output per person.
misconceptions.correction: Check population change too.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a high average as proof every resident benefits.
misconceptions.correction: Examine variation within the population.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical region: real output is 150 million constant-price credits per year and population is 50,000. Calculate annual output per person.
hints: Divide the total by population.
solution: 150,000,000/50,000 = 3,000 constant-price credits per person per year.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical same-currency annual incomes are A: 10, 10, 10, 10 and B: 4, 4, 4, 28 credits. Calculate each mean and explain why the means alone are incomplete.
hints: Compare totals and the individual values.
solution: Both totals are 40 credits across four people, so both means are 10 credits.
B’s distribution is much more uneven than A’s.
Equal means therefore do not establish equal living conditions or distribution.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical claim: a place’s higher HDI score proves it is better on every development dimension for every resident. Evaluate the claim.
hints: A summary index is not every outcome or each person’s experience.
solution: HDI combines selected health, education and income dimensions into an average summary.
A higher overall score need not mean every component or every resident’s outcome is higher.
Inspect components, inequality and other relevant conditions before reaching a broader judgement.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical real output grows from 100 to 110 million credits while population grows from 10,000 to 11,000. Find real output per person before and after.
hints: Divide each total by its corresponding population.
Both totals grow proportionally.
solution: Initially: 100,000,000/10,000 = 10,000 credits per person.
Later: 110,000,000/11,000 = 10,000; output per person is unchanged.

practice.prompt: A region’s average income rises while access to reliable water declines. Can development be said to improve on every dimension?
hints: The two indicators describe different outcomes.
An overall judgement requires explicit criteria.
solution: Income improves on the supplied measure, but reliable-water access worsens.
The evidence contradicts improvement on every dimension; any overall judgement must state how these outcomes are weighed.

notes.title: Distribution shapes the meaning of an average
paragraphs: Development combines economic resources with capabilities and living conditions, so no single average gives a complete account. Real output per person adjusts total production for both prices and population, but it still hides distribution and non-market outcomes. The median identifies the middle observation in ordered data and can differ sharply from the mean when a few values are very high. Comparing both helps describe distribution, although neither reveals every inequality. Education, health, environmental conditions and access to services add other dimensions. Evaluation should specify whose circumstances improved, over what period and by which measures.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical annual incomes are 5, 5, 5, 5 and 30 credits. Find mean and median, then interpret the difference.
steps: Mean = 50/5 = 10 credits.
The middle ordered value is 5 credits, so the median is 5.
workedExamples.conclusion: The high final value raises the mean above the income of most people in this small dataset.

flashcards.front: What does real output per person adjust for?
flashcards.back: Price changes and population size.

flashcards.front: What is the median?
flashcards.back: The middle ordered value, or mean of the two middle values for an even count.

flashcards.front: Why can the mean be misleading about a typical person?
flashcards.back: A few extreme values can pull it away from most observations.

flashcards.front: Does output per person measure every development dimension?
flashcards.back: No; distribution and other outcomes matter.

diagrams.title: Distribution shapes the meaning of an average
diagrams.description: A single high income pulls the mean above the median.

nodes.label: Median
nodes.detail: Middle value 5; most observations lie below the mean

edges.label: compare with the central ordered observation

lessons.summary: Calculate comparative advantage from opportunity costs and distinguish potential gains from their distribution.
objectives: Distinguish absolute and comparative advantage.
Calculate opportunity costs in a two-good model.
Identify mutually beneficial exchange terms under explicit assumptions.
explanation: Absolute advantage concerns producing more with the same resources; comparative advantage concerns giving up less of another good. Calculate each producer’s opportunity cost before assigning comparative advantage. In a simple two-good model with constant trade-offs, the producer with the lower opportunity cost of a good can specialise towards it. A producer can have an absolute advantage in both goods while still having a comparative advantage in only one when opportunity costs differ.

Exchange terms between the two opportunity costs can offer both sides gains relative to producing the imported good themselves. State the direction of the ratio carefully, such as cups per cloth, and identify what each side gives and receives. The simple model assumes resources can be reallocated and ignores some costs. Transport, adjustment, environmental effects and distribution within groups can reduce or redistribute gains. Potential aggregate gains do not prove every worker or household benefits.
keyIdeas: Comparative advantage uses opportunity cost.
Exchange ratios need clear direction and units.
Potential total gains do not guarantee gains for everyone.

definitions.meaning: Ability to produce more output with the same resources in the specified comparison.
Ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost.
The exchange ratio between traded goods, expressed with a clear direction.

method: Read output possibilities for equal resources.
Calculate opportunity costs in both directions.
Assign comparative advantage using the lower cost.
Check an exchange ratio against both costs and state omitted costs.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical equal-resource producers with linear frontiers: A can make 12 cloth units or 6 cups; B can make 8 cloth units or 8 cups. Assess exchanging one cloth unit for 0.75 cup.
steps: For A, one cloth costs 6/12 = 0.5 cup; for B, one cloth costs 8/8 = 1 cup.
A has comparative advantage in cloth and B in cups. The rate 0.75 cup per cloth lies between 0.5 and 1.
A receives 0.75 cup for cloth costing 0.5 cup; B obtains cloth for 0.75 cup instead of its own production cost of 1 cup.
workedExample.conclusion: Both can gain from this exchange under the stated model, with divisible goods and no trade costs. The example does not establish gains for every person within either producer group.

misconceptions.mistake: Choosing comparative advantage from output totals alone.
misconceptions.correction: Compare opportunity costs.

misconceptions.mistake: Reversing a ratio without changing its unit.
misconceptions.correction: State which good is received per unit given.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical linear frontier: a workshop can make 18 bags or 6 stools with the same resources. Find the opportunity cost of one stool in bags.
hints: Use the output forgone per stool.
solution: 18/6 = 3 bags per stool.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical linear frontiers with equal resources: A produces 20 meals or 10 boxes; B produces 12 meals or 12 boxes. Identify comparative advantage for each good.
hints: Compare meals forgone per box.
solution: A’s cost of one box is 20/10 = 2 meals; B’s is 12/12 = 1 meal, so B has comparative advantage in boxes.
A’s cost of one meal is 10/20 = 0.5 box; B’s is 12/12 = 1 box, so A has comparative advantage in meals.

practice.prompt: Using hypothetical costs of 0.5 cup per cloth for A and 1 cup per cloth for B, evaluate A exporting cloth to B at 0.4 cup per cloth, with no other costs or benefits.
hints: Compare the exchange with each producer’s own alternative.
solution: A receives 0.4 cup for cloth that costs it 0.5 cup to produce in opportunity terms.
That rate does not offer A a gain relative to its own production alternative, although it is attractive to B.
For strict mutual gains in this model, the rate must lie above 0.5 and below 1 cup per cloth.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical producer A gives up 3 cups per basket and B gives up 5 cups per basket. Would A exporting one basket for 4 cups benefit both before other costs?
hints: Compare the trade price with each opportunity cost.
Both must beat their domestic trade-off.
solution: A receives 4 cups for a basket costing 3 cups, gaining 1 cup-equivalent.
B pays 4 cups rather than sacrificing 5 to make a basket, so both gain under the assumptions.

practice.prompt: In the previous hypothetical cost structure, A receives 4 cups per exported basket but must spend 2 cups-equivalent on transport. Does A still gain?
hints: Subtract transport from receipts.
Compare net receipts with the 3-cup production cost.
solution: Net receipts = 4 − 2 = 2 cups-equivalent.
This is below A’s 3-cup opportunity cost, so A does not gain under these stated terms and costs.

checklist: I test both sides of an exchange.
I state model and distribution limits.

notes.title: Opportunity cost determines specialisation
paragraphs: Comparative advantage concerns lower opportunity cost, whereas absolute advantage concerns producing more with the same resources. A producer can have absolute advantage in both goods while still benefiting from specialisation and trade under the simple model. Mutually beneficial exchange terms lie between the producers’ opportunity costs, excluding endpoints if both must gain strictly. Transport costs and other barriers can narrow that range. The classroom model assumes comparable goods, usable outputs and the stated resource constraints. It illustrates possible gains rather than proving that every person in each economy benefits equally from actual trade.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical equal-resource frontiers: A makes 24 bowls or 12 plates; B makes 12 bowls or 9 plates. Find comparative advantage.
steps: For A, one plate costs 2 bowls; for B, one plate costs 12/9 = 4/3 bowls.
B has the lower plate cost; A has the lower bowl cost, 1/2 plate versus 3/4 plate.
workedExamples.conclusion: A has absolute advantage in both outputs, yet comparative advantage differs by good.

flashcards.front: What determines comparative advantage?
flashcards.back: Lower opportunity cost.

flashcards.front: What determines absolute advantage?
flashcards.back: Greater output from equivalent resources.

flashcards.front: Where must mutually beneficial terms lie in the simple model?
flashcards.back: Between the parties’ opportunity costs.

flashcards.front: Can transport costs reduce gains from trade?
flashcards.back: Yes; they use resources and narrow the benefit.

diagrams.title: Opportunity cost determines specialisation
diagrams.description: Higher productivity in both goods does not remove relative-cost differences.

nodes.label: Comparative advantage
nodes.detail: B in plates; A in bowls

edges.label: compare the same good’s opportunity cost

lessons.summary: Interpret output, price-level and policy measures while separating nominal changes from real changes.
objectives: Explain GDP as a flow of final production.
Calculate inflation and a real-output measure.
Distinguish fiscal and monetary policy at a conceptual level.
explanation: Macroeconomics studies economy-wide outcomes such as output, inflation and unemployment. Gross domestic product measures the value of final goods and services produced within an economy over a period. Counting both an intermediate input and the full value of the final product would double-count that input. Nominal GDP uses current prices; a real measure adjusts for price changes. Neither output growth nor a larger total alone establishes improved wellbeing for every resident.

Inflation is the rate of increase in a general price index over a stated interval. A fall in the inflation rate can mean prices are still rising more slowly, whereas deflation means the index falls. For these exercises, real GDP equals nominal GDP divided by a GDP deflator expressed with base 100, then multiplied by 100. Fiscal policy concerns government spending and taxation; monetary policy concerns monetary conditions such as interest rates. Their effects depend on conditions and timing, not a guaranteed fixed response.
keyIdeas: GDP is production during a period.
Nominal and real values answer different questions.
Lower positive inflation still means a rising price level.

definitions.meaning: A price measure for domestically produced final output used here as an index with base 100.
Percentage change in a general price index over a specified period.
Government choices about spending and taxation that influence economic activity.

method: Identify the measure, period and price basis.
Exclude double-counting in output reasoning.
Apply the appropriate index or growth calculation.
Interpret direction and distinguish output from wellbeing.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical economy: nominal GDP is 330 million credits and the GDP deflator is 110 with base year 100. Find real GDP in base-year prices.
steps: Use real GDP = nominal GDP × 100/deflator.
330 × 100/110 = 300 million base-year-price credits.
Nominal value includes the price-level effect; the real value removes it using the stated deflator.
workedExample.conclusion: Real GDP is 300 million base-year-price credits. A real growth rate still needs a comparable earlier real GDP value.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling lower positive inflation falling prices.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the price level from its rate of increase.

misconceptions.mistake: Adding every transaction in a production chain to GDP.
misconceptions.correction: Count final output or sum value added consistently.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical annual price index rises from 125 to 130. Calculate inflation over the year.
hints: Use the earlier index as the percentage base.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical real GDP rises from 200 to 210 million constant-price credits. Calculate real growth and explain why nominal GDP is unnecessary for this calculation.
hints: Both values already use the same price basis.
solution: The supplied comparable real values already remove price-level changes; nominal GDP is not needed for this growth calculation.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical inflation falls from 6% in one year to 2% in the next, both measured annually. Explain whether the general price level falls in the second year.
hints: The second rate is still positive.
solution: At 2% inflation, the price index rises by 2% during the second year.
It rises more slowly than under 6% inflation, but it does not fall.
A negative inflation rate would indicate a falling index over the stated interval.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical annual price index rises from 150 to 156. Find inflation and explain the denominator.
hints: Use the increase of six.
Compare it with the earlier index.
solution: The earlier index 150 is the baseline; dividing by 100 would give a different, incorrect growth rate.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical price index falls from 120 to 114. Calculate the change and distinguish it from slower positive inflation.
hints: Retain the negative sign.
A lower index indicates lower basket cost.
solution: This is a falling price level for the index, whereas slower positive inflation would still raise it.

checklist: I state price basis and period.
I calculate with the correct base.
I distinguish growth, prices and wellbeing.

notes.title: Basket cost determines the price index
paragraphs: A price index tracks the cost of a specified basket relative to a base period. Inflation measures the percentage increase in the index between periods, using the earlier index as the denominator. A fall in the inflation rate means prices are rising more slowly, not necessarily falling. The basket’s weights matter because heavily purchased items contribute more to its cost. A fixed basket simplifies comparison but may not reflect later substitution or each household’s spending pattern. Macroeconomic indicators therefore need definitions and context: an economy-wide average can differ from the price changes experienced by a particular household.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical fixed basket contains 2 loaves and 1 milk carton. Prices change from 3 and 4 credits to 4 and 5 respectively. Find basket inflation.
steps: Initial cost = 2 × 3 + 4 = 10 credits; later cost = 2 × 4 + 5 = 13.
workedExamples.conclusion: The result applies to this fixed basket, not every household’s purchases.

flashcards.front: What does a base index of 100 mean?
flashcards.back: The chosen base-period basket cost is represented by 100.

flashcards.front: What is inflation?
flashcards.back: The percentage rise in the general price index over the stated interval.

flashcards.front: Does lower positive inflation mean falling prices?
flashcards.back: No; prices still rise, but more slowly.

flashcards.front: Why do basket weights matter?
flashcards.back: Items purchased in greater quantities have greater cost influence.

diagrams.title: Basket cost determines the price index
diagrams.description: Quantities weight the individual price changes.

lessons.summary: Build an economic response that calculates accurately, distinguishes percentage points from percentages and limits causal claims.
objectives: Select a calculation matched to the question.
Distinguish rate differences from relative changes.
Evaluate data comparability and causal limitations.
explanation: Begin a data response by identifying the source label, time period, population, units and definitions. Decide whether the question needs a level, a difference, a percentage change or a rate. A change from 8% to 6% is a fall of two percentage points, while its relative reduction is one quarter of the initial rate. State the denominator and preserve enough precision to avoid changing the conclusion through early rounding.

Use calculations as evidence within an explanation, not as a substitute for one. A simultaneous policy change and improved outcome do not by themselves identify a causal effect. Check whether definitions, coverage, prices or population changed and consider other influences. Distinguish hypothetical exercise data from observed statistics. A strong judgement answers the task while explaining what further evidence would be needed to generalise, compare fairly or attribute an outcome to a specific intervention.
keyIdeas: The question determines the denominator.
Percentage points and percent changes differ.
Association alone does not identify policy effects.

definitions.meaning: The arithmetic difference between two percentages expressed in percentage points.
The change divided by the initial value, multiplied by 100.
The extent to which measures share definitions, coverage and other conditions needed for a valid comparison.

method: Read metadata and define the requested measure.
Write the formula with a stated denominator.
Calculate, retain units and interpret direction.
Evaluate comparability, alternative explanations and scope.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical unemployment rate falls from 8% to 6% under an unchanged definition. Calculate the percentage-point change and relative percentage change.
steps: Percentage-point change = 6 - 8 = -2 percentage points.
Relative change = (6 - 8)/8 × 100 = -25%.
Both describe the same rate movement in different units; the rates alone do not establish the change in the number unemployed if the labour force changed.
workedExample.conclusion: The rate falls by 2 percentage points, or 25% relative to its starting level. Report the unit to avoid confusing these statements.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing a percentage-point difference as the relative percent change.
misconceptions.correction: Use the initial value as denominator for a relative change.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a before-and-after comparison as causal proof.
misconceptions.correction: Consider other changes and a suitable comparison before attributing effects.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical participation rate rises from 40% to 50% with the same definition. Calculate the percentage-point increase and relative percentage increase.
hints: Compare the difference with the starting rate.
solution: Increase = 50 - 40 = 10 percentage points.
Relative increase = 10/40 × 100 = 25%.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical spending rises from 100 to 121 million credits while the relevant same-base price index rises from 100 to 110. Find final real spending in base-year prices and real growth.
hints: Adjust the later nominal value before comparing.
solution: Final real spending = 121 × 100/110 = 110 million base-year-price credits.
Initial real spending = 100 million in the base year.
Real growth = (110 - 100)/100 × 100 = 10%, compared with 21% nominal growth.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical data show unemployment falling after a training programme starts. No comparison group or information about wider demand is supplied. Evaluate the claim that the programme caused the entire fall.
hints: What else might change employment?
solution: The timing is consistent with a programme effect but does not isolate it.
Wider labour demand, labour-force changes or other policies could contribute.
Use comparable outcomes, programme participation evidence and an appropriate comparison while checking definitions before attributing the entire fall.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical survey A has 30 satisfied respondents out of 50; B has 90 out of 150. Find the combined satisfaction rate.
hints: Add satisfied counts and total respondents separately.
Use the combined fraction.
solution: Satisfied = 120; respondents = 200.
Combined rate = 120/200 × 100% = 60%.

practice.prompt: Two regions each have an output index of 120 with base 100. Does this prove their current output levels are equal?
hints: Indices compare each region with its own base.
Absolute base outputs may differ.
solution: Both have risen 20% relative to their respective bases.
Their absolute outputs can differ because the base levels are not supplied; equal indices do not establish equal size.

notes.title: Combined rates need denominator weights
paragraphs: Economic data comparisons require aligned definitions, populations, dates and units. Combining percentages from differently sized groups requires weighting by their denominators. A simple average of rates gives each group equal weight even when one contains many more people. Rebased indices can aid comparison, but indices show relative movement rather than absolute size. Graphs should identify truncated axes and the interval covered, because visual steepness can change without any change in the underlying data. A strong response performs the relevant calculation, describes what it establishes and separates that descriptive result from an unsupported causal explanation.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical groups: A has 10 unemployed people in a labour force of 100; B has 10 in a labour force of 400. Find the combined rate.
steps: Combined unemployed = 20; combined labour force = 500.
workedExamples.conclusion: Averaging 10% and 2.5% would wrongly weight unequal labour forces equally.

flashcards.front: How are group rates combined correctly?
flashcards.back: Add numerators and denominators, then calculate the rate.

flashcards.front: What does an index mainly show?
flashcards.back: Relative change from a stated base.

flashcards.front: Why inspect a graph’s axis range?
flashcards.back: Truncation can exaggerate apparent differences.

flashcards.front: Does a before-and-after pattern alone prove policy causation?
flashcards.back: No; other changes may explain it.

diagrams.description: The larger group contributes more people to the total.
